name: Name
body: 623 AR "Captain Rosko! We’ve just crossed the river." The Sky Corps captain, dressed in polished armor, saluted and snapped his heels as swift winds howled around them. "Dorset Valley is upon us." Caught in the act of her pre-battle ritual, Cynthia "Cyn" Rosko was obliged to lean over the rail atop the deck of the Invader skyship, the Furious Finn, despite her adjutant’s report, whereupon she heaved bile into the literal fog of war below. Her nausea abated. She cracked her neck, stretched both arms out, and patted both of her arcanely enhanced shoulder pauldrons before bringing her hands back together with a whispered prayer to anyone listening. After fifteen drops, she had her routine; it would be bad luck to skip any part of it, no matter who was looking her way. "Randolph, right?" Cyn wiped her mouth and turned with a smirk to regard the stern adjutant. "Ma’am," the young captain nodded; he looked pained as he waited for her to speak. Cynthia squinted at the rakish Midlunder. He had a narrow face and a hawkish nose. Highborn, by the looks of him. Not necessarily a problem. The fact that she hadn’t dropped with him before was of minor concern. Indeed, based on his record, this would be only his second combat drop. Randolph was a last-minute assignment to the Furious Finn’s flight on account of her last adjutant taking a spear to the face just a week ago.

name: Name
body: "Yes, ma’am." "Breathe, why don’t you?" Cynthia took a breath of her own over the rush of open air, extending a gauntlet his way. "Call me Cyn while you’re at it. We’re both captains. I’m not one for formality." "Yes, Ma…Cynthia." Randolph put his hand forward. "I’m Dekker." Cynthia pulled his hand in for a quick shake. "Second drop, eh?" "Is it that obvious?" Dekker swallowed, forcing himself to smile. "Try to loosen up." Cynthia looked back out over the rail to the low clouds below, brushing a whitened lock of her hair behind one ear. Below, an ocean of low-hanging clouds ran to the ends of the horizon. Sparse hilltops cleared the cover here and there, but the peaks gave her crew all the direction they needed to navigate. "It’s about to get messy." Behind the Furious Finn’s steady pace of thirty knots, two more Invaders followed in an echelon wing formation spread out at fifty-yard intervals. As with the Furious Finn, the Jolly Dodger and the Cracker Barrel were loaded for bear with troops, warjacks, and guns. Lots of guns. The signature dual-prow design of their combat transports sailed the skies with all the authority that their bristling belly cannons granted. Indeed, Cynthia had been granted command of no less than a full-strength flight, laden with a platoon of Cygnar’s finest to reinforce the line at Merin’s northwest gates against the ongoing Orgoth invasion. Of course, they were nowhere to be seen beneath the cloud cover, but Cynthia could read the battle below well enough. Under those clouds and the rain, in the gloom of a battle on mud-slicked ground, the guns raged as she looked on. A cannon report lit a cloud starboard, followed by a deep thud. Another to port. And so on. She could identify the armies by the report of the guns: the rolling roar of Ordic cannons and the tortured shrieking of their Orgoth counterpart. Cynthia closed her eyes, reaching out with senses honed by her warcaster training. The din of battle carried skyward as they passed over shouting, gunfire, and the bellow of Orgoth warjacks below.

name: Name
body: The Orgoth raiders were moving fast, that much was sure, picked at here and there by allied skirmishers and distant artillery to wither their flanks and herd them into a kill box. Still, the stampede of armored men and machines seemed unconcerned by the goading, all the more riled to take Ord’s capital and raze it to the ground. Yet Cynthia’s Khadoran counterparts in the valley ahead were mortar batteries, a company of Winter Korps, and squads of concealed snipers along the northern hillside ruins to receive them. The Khadorans had only recently dug in, but they were well placed to create a slaughtering field in the path of the Orgoth assault. As the Furious Finn descended, the clouds thinned to wisps, just enough to reveal the Orgoth horde rushing below. Merin was a squat city of some eighty thousand people, built along a wide river that meandered through sprawling farmlands and surrounded by rolling hills. The invaders had held course in a straight line, aimed for the heart of the city through the narrowing pass of Dorset Valley. Once Cynthia’s force landed on the south side of the valley, their trap would be complete.

name: Name
body:
As they moved ever-closer into position, the cloud cover sealed back up, though Cynthia had seen enough. She had already glimpsed Merin’s west gates, reinforced with ramparts and gun batteries alike. Dorset Valley was preciously close to Merin; the fight would be upon them soon enough if allied forces here fell. Frantic refugees were already evacuating the city as a precaution through the eastern gates.
Dekker followed her gaze into the clouds, flinching when an airburst shell pierced the clouds. It was followed by a telltale thud-thud-BOOM report.
"Relax." Cyn smiled, turning toward the skyship’s helm. "Borisyuk and his mortars have range."
"We should be about over the drop zone," Dekker announced.
"On me." Cynthia was already moving with purposeful strides down to the upper deck. The stacks of her steam-powered armor’s boiler left wisps of smoke trailing behind her. As she moved, she felt the tug of another presence in the hold below. It was her warjack, Pokey. While not the most fearsome of names, it certainly suited him. Since the pair had bonded, he was always pestering her, always poking for attention. Owing to a hold packed tight with guns and supplies, Pokey was the sole warjack in her retinue today.

name: Name
body: Now? Pokey’s mind pressed at her. The warjack didn’t communicate with words but with urges and emotional waves she had learned to interpret over their years together. Almost, she thought back. "Ma’am." Sergeant Baxter nodded from his place along the Furious Finn’s gunwales. His squad of Gravediggers was with him. It was the same troop she’d dropped with last time, minus a few faces. "Your grunts ready?" Cyn kept walking even as she addressed her sergeant. Baxter nodded with a bitter smile. "To the last." "Good. Time to go below. Let’s give them hell down there!" she shouted over the rising thrum of the ship’s sky drives. Punctuating her rallying cry, a flare burst through the clouds amidst a cacophony of shell blasts below. Brilliant crimson, three hundred meters to the south. It hung there a moment, blinding, then fizzled and fell back into the clouds, spent. Dekker shook his head. "Blasted reds." "Have your helmsman take us below the cloud cover." Cynthia shook her head along with her sergeant. Indeed, the signal was not welcome. Among the variety of flare semaphore shared between Cygnar’s forces and the Khadorans, this one was the worst. It meant the plan was already going sideways; Khador’s flank was in danger of folding on the other side of the valley. "I need to see what’s happening."

name: Name
body: Dekker nodded, making for the bridge to the Furious Finn’s aft. Her flight followed suit, keeping formation. In short order, the cloud bank was above them, and the battlefield lay exposed in a sweeping view to either end of the horizon. As the Furious Finn moved for their south-side position, Cynthia shook her head again. "They’re not moving for the gate." She produced a spyglass from her belt and studied the horde in detail and then their destination. Indeed, they had diverted for the Khadoran position. She studied the ancient ruins the Khadorans had hunkered down in. Excellent cover, yes, but the ruins were Orgoth in origin. Her stomach again began to churn as she looked to them, an old intuition creeping into her thoughts. She glanced to the forest line adjacent the ruins. "Fek me. They’re not here for Merin. Not yet." Alongside her, Baxter quailed. "What do you mean?" "Follow me." Cynthia was already moving for the bridge.

name: Name
body: Standing next to his helmsman within the cramped bridge, Dekker monitored the ship’s flight instruments. "We’re ready to drop, Captain," he announced, looking up as Cynthia approached. "Like hell we are," Cynthia said. "Come about." "Captain?" Dekker was confused. "Our orders are clear." "Change of plans. The Orgoth aren’t moving for Merin. They’re going for the ruins." Dekker nodded as if this made perfect sense. "Where do you want us?" "The trees. There." Cynthia pointed beyond the port-side window of the bridge. "We need to support Borisyuk’s troops." "That will leave the gates vulnerable," Dekker protested, confused. "I thought our mission—" "Look for yourself, man," Cynthia snapped. "They aren’t moving for the gates. I think… No, I sense…there’s something more to those ruins than meets the eye. Whoever is leading those reavers—I think they know this, too." "Yes, Captain." At once, the helmsman followed her lead. The sturdy frame of the Furious Finn groaned as he turned the wheel. In turn, her flight held formation and began to move for the tree line alongside the ruins. As the flight passed over the stampede at an altitude of only a hundred and fifty feet , Cynthia looked to Dekker.

name: Name
body: "Let’s make those bastards regret setting foot on Immorese soil again." She smiled grimly. "Yes, ma’am." He grabbed the wired relay to the gunner cupola’s and shouted with a gleam in his eye, "All stations, open fire!" In short order, the Jolly Dodger and the Cracker Barrel took their turns, each Invader strafing the line of foul men and seething machines with the clap and bang of rolling thunder. Deep craters erupted where their cannons struck, throwing up a slurry of blood, mud, guts, and twisted metal. Yet the enemy would not be cowed. There was a feral cry from somewhere within the center of the horde, an entirely unnerving pitch. Cynthia felt the Gift in that howl, unmistakable. It seemed to rile them all the more, as they pressed on, snarling, clambering over their dead and up the slopes with reckless abandon. "Dekker, signal our plan to the others," Cyn ordered, her tone sharpening. "Baxter, let’s get the troops ready to debark." "We need altitude for our chutes to open." Baxter winced as if realizing he was stating the obvious. "We’re not nearly high enough."

name: Name
body: "There’s no time for that now." Cynthia cleared her throat. "We have just enough of a lead to put down and form a battle line and then get the Invaders clear. Let’s get below." "This is going to be close," Dekker agreed, looking to the Orgoth advance before following Cynthia below deck. "But I think you’re right." In the cargo hold, her Gravediggers held their weapons and braced themselves against the interior of the hull. Cynthia regarded them with pride and adrenaline both. She looked to her flight’s wake and there saw a wide enough lead to offload, but only just. Beneath the Furious Finn, a thick oak grove sloped, overlooking the Khadoran position with a sixty-yard no-man’s-land between them. As the skyships descended, the Khadoran position continued to hammer away at the enemy, belching smoke and dealing death by mortar and sniper alike all along the range of the feral advance. And still the Orgoth came closer, uglier and stranger by the yard as their chains, their blaze-fueled weapons, and their grimly adorned masks came into view. As the telltale howl in their press sounded again, their energy became even more manic and overwhelming. Cynthia shook it off, focused on the battle to come and, with it, the welling of magic in her own chest.

name: Name
body: "Aah." She cringed, that nagging nausea hitting her again as they descended. She looked to the ruins, and felt the sickness of an all-too familiar and most shameful of tastes: a soul. It manifested on her tongue as syrupy sweet. A taste beckoning. There was no denying the waft of the place from this range. She fought it back, tensing her jaw against the task. Focusing her mind, she unshouldered her rocket launcher, checked it with a tilt, then slapped the side shield just to be sure. "Ready platoon," she shouted, every eye in the hold on her. "Form a battle line against the trees, on my position!" At once, each Invader touched down, mooring stabilizers spread wide to steady the crafts as they hovered just above the earth. Gangways in the stern of the ships lowered to the ground, disgorging Gravediggers, artillery, and supply crates that were quickly sorted into an efficient line. An unchained Pokey came stomping out of the Furious Finn’s hold, the steam from his boiler forming an unmistakable growl. As befitted a Valiant class, he banged his hammer above the gun barrel protruding from his volley shield and vented steam from the sides of his face grill. The hastily mounted heavy cannon atop his carapace traversed to target the enemy, settling down slope. Behind him emerged a field gun crew, and down the line, the remaining Invaders unloaded crewed weapons of their own. As each skyship settled in, the fast-forming fire line of soldiers and guns took their place and readied their weapons.

name: Name
body: Cynthia was on the ground and into the fray at the center of the line. She quickly dropped to one knee and gazed through her iron sights, the oversized weapon tracing an arc down-range and downhill. The horde was closing, but they had a moment yet. "Hurry!" She pointed as Baxter and his men took their places beside her, priming smoke bombs and setting gun sights. "Get those Invaders up and give them thunder!" Overhead, Dekker nodded, bringing the flight round for another strafing run. Their dust covered the firing line with a groan of their sky drives, then they were moving again, looking for a firing solution while climbing. The attack would not get far. Up and out of the trees erupted a dozen Rhok Harriers with bloodcurdling screams: the Orgoth’s great winged beasts, each one several yards in length from beak to tail, all clawed and fanged. They had arrived skulking in the trees but were now ready to strike. "Fek." Cynthia watched her flight take evasive action before they could fire a shot. Up they climbed, lost to the air battle. She watched them wheel away from the massive reptilian creatures but not before they were able to grapple with the Jolly Dodger. In short order, she saw the Invader tilt as three Rhoks clawed and gnashed at the gyro rings of the portside sky drive, shredding them until the drive exploded in an arcane pulse that exploded like a voltaic grenade followed by a torrent of sparks. The Invader’s flight crew fired pistols at the creatures to repel them but to no avail; maimed, the Invader soon lost control, rolling toward its port side as it plummeted for the ground directly over the Khadoran position. It was a devastating impact that shook the soil beneath her feet, crushing a mortar team under cover and a Dire Wolf warjack in the open at the same time.

name: Name
body:
Cynthia cursed aloud as a plume of black smoke spewed from the broken hull of the Invader. The ship had come down hard; she knew there was no chance any of the crew could have survived. Their deaths gnawed at her guts, and she clenched her teeth in anger.
Down the line, her Gravediggers watched with grim determination as the foul Orgoth moved ever closer on the Khadorans, just out of range but quickly closing the gap.
"Set those guns!" Cynthia shouted, watching the artillery crews scramble to deploy the mobile field guns on either side of her down the line. "The bastards are almost on top of them."
The rising tide of flesh, armor, and jagged steel closed in endless waves it seemed, pointed unerringly at the Khadorans. Their enemy came into focus as the distance shrank. Wave after wave of assault reavers, skirmishers, and strike reavers, all wearing ornate armor and wielding wicked curved blades and flame-belching firearms, barreled in. Behind them, a trio of Siege Tarasks lumbered along—tusked brutes, twelve feet tall with ghastly harpoons lashed to their armored backs, each crewed by a savage raider saddled atop the beast.

name: Name
body:
To the center of the press, Cynthia saw the Orgoth warjacks driven forward now: a pair each of the Tyrants and Jackals that had become familiar elements in any engagement with the Invaders. She took a breath and readied for range. She could not sense where their warcaster was among their ranks, but she knew they could not be far from their warjacks.
"They could take the pass." Baxter marveled at their focus. "Why advance through the ruins?"
"Something bad in there." Cynthia grimaced, glancing down her sights as Pokey, eager for battle, loomed behind her. "Something buried down deep."
Baxter’s expression turned bleak as he glanced at all of his Gravediggers down the line. "I’ll have to take your word for it, ma’am."
Cynthia watched as the artillery crews signaled readiness with upraised arms. There was no time to spare. She compelled Pokey to come alongside, focusing through his eyes as he trained the heavy cannon on his back to fire at the heart of the horde.
"Open fire!" she commanded, infusing the payload within her mechanika rocket launcher Witch Hammer with her arcane power as she pulled the trigger.  Glitter-laced fire and incandescent runes swirled beyond the ponderous barrel as the explosive round found its mark in the center of the horde’s advance.

name: Name
body: The Gravediggers answered her call, one and all. Next to Cynthia, Pokey braced as his gun rocked a barrage of fire, ending life after worthless life with each shell’s fiery impact. The field guns fired one after another; the clank-clank recoil of each sounded like a hammer to an anvil. One by one, they burst into the heart of the rush, sending up eruptions of earth, blood, steel, and gore, each impact a blinding flashpoint and a crater cleared of life. Among the violent blasts, a Siege Tarask was rocked by fire from two guns simultaneously, sending it stumbling to the ground and crushing its rider as it rolled onto its back. Yet the advance continued. They would not be stopped now. Each crater formed was soon lost to the primal rush. "Morrow’s sake, do they feel anything?" Baxter grimaced as he gripped his rifle, firing while the enemy persisted in its advance. Down the line, a steady rhythm fell into place as each Gravedigger fired, reloaded, took aim, and fired again. Above, Dekker’s surviving flight circled the battle, guns blazing to defeat the Rhok Harriers. As above, so below: the battle was one deafening volley after another. The kill box had been formed at last with the Khadorans. It was now fully engaged.

name: Name
body:
But the Orgoth shoved forward, their leading edge only twenty yards from the Khadorans, no matter how many lives their mortars claimed getting there. The withering fire had slowed the raiders, raising Cynthia’s hopes that the horde might yet be turned back. Then, the warjacks were spurred ahead, with the Tyrants bounding after the quicker Jackals in the lead. Their strange designs and heavy blades were quickly inside the Khadoran line, fiery guns blazing. No shots could stop them it seemed. Not now.
"Machine guns, on their point!" Cynthia shouted over the din, directing attention to the front of the advance. She watched the stampede, reavers and skirmishers alike following up after their warjacks, most cut down, butchered in the crossfire.
Each of the Gravedigger machine gun positions lit up, spitting white hot death, tearing through the waves of raiders down range. The steady barrage they traced over no-man’s-land raked the Orgoth back wherever it led.
Killed over and again, the Orgoth either did not appear to sense their danger or simply did not care. To Cynthia, Orgoth casualties seemed endless and endlessly stepped over. Given the rampaging warjacks that had overrun the Khadorans’ position, however, something had to be done.

name: Name
body: "Whatever it takes." Cynthia looked over at her sergeant, reloading. "Make sure they hold the ruins." "Yes, ma’am." Baxter nodded, firing his rifle. Who is commanding them? Cynthia wondered, glimpsing someone or something as a mercurial blur in the rush. Whoever they were, it seemed they led with feral howls, steady screaming, and magic. In the end, it didn’t matter. The Khadorans needed support. Cynthia looked at the nearest Tyrant and cracked her neck. "We’ve got a target, Pokey." She looked to her ’jack and he to her. We kill, he implored her. "Hold the line, Sergeant," she ordered, checking her pouch for a signaling flare. "I suggest yeh don’t stop shooting until they’re all dead." "You want us to cover you, Captain?" Baxter looked at the rampaging Tyrants with apprehension. "Signal the Invaders to come about." Cynthia glanced up at the flight as she loaded a new rocket into Witch Hammer. "If they can get clear of those Rhoks, I’m going to mark a target for them." "Yes, ma’am." Baxter raised a flare pistol and put a burst of brilliant blue into the sky overhead. "Good hunting."

name: Name
body:
Sprinting, Cynthia charged toward the Orgoth warjacks with Pokey stomping behind her in tow. She tapped her Gift, summoning shadows ahead with a spell, vanishing into them and stepping into a new space on the other side. Here and then there she ran, focused. Every second counted now.
The Khadoran defenders, meanwhile, were down to their last Dire Wolf—until a Tyrant took its head clean off with a grinding blow from its ripper blade. Then, they were fighting the mechanikal terrors hand to hand. The Tyrants plowed through the men, reaping death with every sweep of their great bladed limbs. The Jackals, too, lent fire to the fray, slaying one Khadoran after another.
The warjacks’ advance, as Cynthia saw it, had moved toward a central point of the ruins, a concentric design. Worn pillars surrounded them now, forming an arena.
In range at last, she braced her stance, raised her weapon, and stared down her sights as she guided her warjack to open fire first. Pokey eagerly obliged, firing at the closest of the Jackals. With her arcanely enhanced rocket aimed at the second Jackal, she let loose and moved on when the vile thing stumbled to the ground, headless.

name: Name
body:
It took her three strides to find cover and reload. The reavers were closing in despite grievous losses inflicted by her field guns. She was running out of room to move but needed to buy time. Reaching into a hip pouch, she produced a signal flare and ignited it, sending a plume of purple smoke skyward that would direct their attention to her target. She hoped the crews of the Invaders were watching. Meanwhile, a Tyrant laid waste to a unit of cornered Khadoran snipers, and Cynthia lined the thing up in her sights.
"Pick on someone yer own size." She fired. Her rocket traced rings of glittery runes down the length of its travel until it impacted in the center of the Tyrant’s core. It fell back at once, stumbling and spewing blaze around it.
Overhead, the Invaders responded. Two volleys of cannon fire struck the staggered warjack, blasting it and everything within a few yards apart. Masonry went flying; dust and smoke blotted the sky. Cynthia wasted no time reloading and hit the other Tyrant in its power plant, bursting steam pipes with her rocket. As another Invader attack fired upon the Tyrant, it was helpless to avoid the fire and was soon blown to pieces.

name: Name
body: Just as the last Tyrant was extinguished, Cynthia sensed its controller at the edge of her consciousness. It was the Orgoth warcaster known as Kishtaar, the one called the Howling Silence, an adversary she’d faced many times since the initial invasion but one who had eluded her opponents time and again. As quickly as she could feel her presence, however, the enemy warcaster retreated. A shrieking call echoed through the ranks of the raiders, and they turned to run, withdrawing to the slopes and the forests below. Cynthia wondered what had triggered the enemy commander to backpedal after all she and her forces had lost and with no apparent gain. The Khadorans were nearly spent, too. Indeed, the end was so sudden, so total, it seemed almost surreal to her. She stood slowly, wondering where they were going. She watched as the Gravediggers fired after them, and the remaining Khadorans recovered. She looked then to the smoking wreck of the Jolly Dodger amongst the ruins. Beside her, Pokey scanned downslope, looking for stragglers in range of its cannon. There were none.

name: Name
body:
For now, it seemed the battle had been won.
***

name: Name
body:
"Captain, you’re going to want to see this." Baxter waved to Cynthia as she paced the perimeter of the ruins or what was left of them after the Jolly Dodger had crashed, still scanning for danger.
She looked across the field of gore and metal that had resulted from the battle then toward the shattered rock that held the sergeant’s attention. Her junior officer, Lieutenant Stella Barron, and one of her corporals had brought forth a leather case that she had carried aboard the Furious Finn. "There’s something here, ma’am. It could be what the CRS had us on the lookout for."
Cynthia looked to her lieutenant with apprehension. "What is it?"
"These old Ordic ruins were sitting on top of something even older. Something Orgoth, by the looks of it." Baxter poked a rift in the ruins with his bayonet. "There’s an opening. And a foul wind coming out of it. Could be a chamber below."
"For Morrow’s sake," Cynthia groused at his efforts, pausing a step. The spot radiated with the sickly-sweet taste of souls. Though no one else could sense it, it was all she could do not to be sick. "I knew it."

name: Name
body:
"I brought this out, ma’am." Barron indicated the Orgoth case. "In case this is what we think it is."
"I don’t suppose we can bury it again?" Cynthia joked then sighed.
Next, Barron turned to her squad and waved them over. "You grunts! The captain needs your help."
Cynthia fought back the growing gag reflex she felt provoked by the object within the case and opened it with a deep breath.  When she did, she drew out an Orgoth key and studied it. It seethed with energy now, an indication it was indeed meant to interface with something below. In appearance, it was stone, a three-foot long scepter that seemed to twist in her grip yet was light to carry.
Baxter squinted into the fissure in the ruins. "I see stairs leading down."
"Yeh don’t say." Cynthia returned the obelisk to its casing and drew near as the Gravediggers began to clear the opening wide enough to enter.
"The Invader must have cracked opened the ceiling." Baxter joined her side, visibly impressed. "It’s huge down there, whatever it is."

name: Name
body: "Fek me," Cynthia swore, realizing her fear of this place was now inescapable. She gazed into the revealed shaft, its depth seemingly endless with only a circular stairwell spiraling down the wall into blackness. The way was obstructed, but from what she could see, there were Orgoth glyphs carved into the wall all the way down. They seemed to glow faintly with the incoming light. "We’re going down there, aren’t we?" Stella looked down, apprehensively. "Maybe." Cynthia shrugged, resigned. "Okay, definitely. Get some picks to clear the way. Hooks, ropes, and lanterns, too." "Right away, ma’am." Baxter quickly ordered one of the Gravediggers to run back to the waiting Furious Finn. "Whatever is down there, the Orgoth wanted it very badly." Cynthia looked to Barron and around the circle of her troopers. "Let’s make sure it’s not here when they return." Around her, the Gravediggers nodded, their purpose resolved. The remainder of Cynthia’s flight was soon gathered overhead, holding station as supplies were lowered. Her platoon meanwhile formed a defensive perimeter around the shaft. As she chose her descent party, a curious detachment of Khadorans approached, led by a weary-looking Khadoran warcaster covered in furs and skins and sporting a notably long beard.

name: Name
body:
Cynthia marked his approach with a nod. "Kapitan Borisyuk."
"My thanks to you, Captain." Borisyuk nodded in return, adjusting the exceptionally large sniper rifle at his shoulder. "I am thankful for your support. I thought we would not survive the day."
"Happy to oblige." Cynthia’s gaze returning to watch her troopers chipping away at the masonry to open the shaft wide enough to enter.
"You will forgive me to ask, what is the meaning of this?" Borisyuk leaned in to stare down the shaft.
"It seems the battle has revealed something under these old ruins. Our reconnaissance service had reason to believe that there might be a significant Orgoth cache in the vicinity. Something possibly related to this artifact the sent us out here with." She held up the scepter. "They love chasing down all these six-hundred-year-old crypts and vaults, but we’re the ones that have to do the dirty work. So, we’re investigating."
"Interesting." Borisyuk scratched his beard, intrigued.
"Seems there’s something to it, though. I believe it’s the reason they came at you so hard." Cynthia looked on as the opening grew larger. "Do yeh feel the foulness of this place?"

name: Name
body: "There is a presence," Borisyuk agreed, closing his eyes. "It is unknown to me." "I wish I could say the same." Cynthia crossed her arms as the Gravediggers’ picks struck again. "Then I should very much like to see for myself." Borisyuk looked to the abyss as the Gravediggers pried away the last obstructions. Cynthia’s team was chosen at last. "Follow us down if you like, but I won’t blame you if you don’t. You know as well as I do that you never know what you’ll find in these old Orgoth hell pits." "Indeed, I do." Borisyuk waved a dour sniper and a hefty-looking soldier to his side from amongst his battered troops. "We will follow." The way before them clear, Cynthia took up a torch and led the descent. The air that filled her nostrils was foul, sulfurous. She felt Pokey slip away with each step, pressing for her to let him follow. No, she insisted with her thoughts. I’ll call for you if I need you. Down she went, her footfalls echoing into the darkness. At intervals there were door wells in the stairs, yet a wider chamber seemed to open below and almost beckoned to her heightened senses. There were souls down here. An abundance of them. She felt their taste again. The deeper she went, the more her skin crawled.

name: Name
body:
"What is this that makes the air so thick?" Alongside her, Borisyuk swallowed.
"Souls." Cynthia looked ahead to find an arched doorway, pointed to it. "This place is bursting with souls."
Borisyuk grimaced. "Death, I have seen plenty. But never so…concentrated."
Cynthia took a breath, putting foot after foot until at last they hit bottom. The way forward now led to a pair of intact doors. The Orgoth key she carried practically surged at this range. When they reached the tall entryway, she found a lock clearly ready made for the Orgoth scepter.
"Of course." She pressed the scepter into the socket created for it, feeling the pair connect with a surge of energy. At once, the double doors swung open, revealing a vaulted chamber beyond. Oddly, her lamp was no longer necessary. Whatever was down here glowed bright enough for all to see; the widening chamber opening to a buttressed ceiling nearly a hundred feet overhead.
Around the chamber wall were numerous arcades, all conducting oddly humming pipes. They ran everywhere, yet all of them were aligned to the center of the chamber. At intervals between the pipes, Cynthia counted twelve metal cylinders the size of coffins, crafted from ornate, metal latticework. These were soul cages—and the sight of them only increased her nausea. Ancient souls trapped within them were being slowly siphoned as fuel to sustain a roiling field of energy enshrouding something indistinct atop a basalt dais in the dead center of the cavernous vault. Carvings were visible everywhere now, unmistakably Orgoth. They covered the walls, the floor, and the ceiling. Weapons and other strange artifacts of intricate design and unimaginable effect hung from every wall. All seemed to pulse with the chamber’s force, though it was ultimately channeled to the central ball of energy most of all.

name: Name
body: "I have been in Orgoth places. Many have been uncovered in Khador." Borisyuk looked on in amazement at the rippling sphere of energy. "Never like this."

name: Name
body:
At once, the pressure of the place became palpable. As Cynthia glanced behind Borisyuk to Baxter and the rest of her party, she found them shaking, almost frozen. Whatever reaction it gave her and her fellow warcaster, she knew it inflicted ten times the effect on the mundane.
"Stay back," Cynthia ordered Baxter. "All of you, back to the stairwell."
A visibly shaken Baxter squinted after her. "Are you sure?"
"Those are soul cages." Cynthia pointed at the arcades and the cages within them. "They’re powering that thing. If your head hurts now, it’s only going to get worse in a minute."
Seeing his apprehension, she gestured again. "Go on, Sergeant. We’ll be all right."
"Aye, Captain." Baxter retreated.
"What do you suppose it is?" Borisyuk whispered, his eyes locked on the swirling ball.
"It contains something. Maybe shielding it." Cynthia shook her head, slowly approaching the dais, now bathed in the light as it transitioned between colors known and unknown. Deep down, her nausea was giving way to an appetite. The exposure was intoxicating—as it had been once before when she had been lured. It was an appetite given her by her time in Skell so many years ago. The Orgoth, as with Cryx, fed upon souls, and she too had been afflicted with that taste. It pulled at her now, and she could not deny it.

name: Name
body:
"She is all right, Kapitan?" Borisyuk’s sniper escort tugged at his shoulder.
"She is fine." Borisyuk watched as Cynthia led on. "Do as she says and stay back."
Cynthia paid them no attention, stepping onto the dais as if entranced. Her appetite grew, though she resisted. Yet it became clear what she must do. At last in front of the shifting energy field, she stared at it and raised one hand. She took off her gauntlet and flexed her bare hand a moment.
"Captain, are you sure that’s wise?" Borisyuk asked behind her.
"We do as we must," Cynthia murmured, resigned.
Then she put her hand into the swirl of color. Light flooded the room in blinding brilliance, coruscating waves in a kaleidoscope, though she did not notice. Her hand touched metal within the sphere, a surface covered in intricate relief that sent chills down her spine. The moment she made contact with the object within, the energy field dissipated. The chamber fell dark. Somewhere in the shadows, a creaking groan echoed like a ship run aground. Cynthia turned to see Borisyuk opening the baffles on his lantern.

name: Name
body:
"What is it?" he whispered.
Cynthia traced her hand across the surface of a sphere as wide as a warjack, formed of interlocking plates covered in twisted, grotesque patterns and anguished faces characteristic of Orgoth design. Its purpose was uncertain. Seams between the plates, joints, and sockets around the sphere suggested the possibility that it might be articulated, could possibly open, or might even be some strange form of mechanika. It pulsed dimly within, emitting a spectral green light.
"We need to get this out of here." Cynthia peered around the chamber. "All of these weapons too."
Yet she could not detach her gaze from the orb.
"Are you well?" Borisyuk looked on. "It seems to have a hold on you. You seem unable to let go."
"I don’t know," Cynthia admitted. "What I do know is this place was made to contain it. There are over a thousand souls in this place."
She could feel a distant vibration with each of the sphere’s eerie pulses. She traced a finger over sigils etched into its surface, noting they were repeated along the walls of the chamber, and now they all pulsed in time with the same glow as the mysterious orb. So much raw power…

name: Name
body:
"Let us not waste time then," Borisyuk urged. "This is a significant task ahead, and our mutual enemy could return at any time."
"Good advice," Cynthia said, closing her eyes as she willed herself to step away from the sphere.
"What is it do you think?" Borisyuk stared at it as long as he could as they ascended the stairwell.
"Something they want." Cynthia frowned. "And that’s enough, isn’t it?"
***
Kapitan Ilari Borisyuk led the remains of his detachment back to the regimental field camp east of Merin. As he walked, he was met from the other side of the road by Kapitan Vonesk and a stamping pair of imposing heavy warjacks—Great Bears—followed by a line of Winter Korps that stretched on for another fifty yards in double files. Behind the soldiers came a group of three mortars with crew and ammunition wagons. That had been his detachment strength only that morning, give or take. Now, he had maybe half as many. No artillery, no warjacks. Only stragglers from a battle that had gone very badly, indeed.

name: Name
body:
As Borisyuk’s detachment withdrew, Vonesk would reinforce his position and once again secure the northern approach to the besieged city of Merin. Though his losses were grievous, and his heart was heavy to think upon them, in the end, the line had held. They had won this day, even helped deny the Orgoth access to potentially invaluable ancient relics. As a soldier of Khador, what more could be asked of him? Given the casualties on the other side, he and his men would no doubt receive appropriate commendations.
Yet Borisyuk was too tired for good news. As he thought about the battle, the Cygnaran captain, Cynthia Rosko, had certainly lived up to her reputation. Indeed, her quick thinking had proven both a spectacle and a blessing. There was no doubt in his mind that he and his surviving troops may well have been wiped from Immoren without her intervention.
More than this, Borisyuk had seen Rosko come alive in those final moments of battle, possessed of a magic he knew in his bones she should not have. The soul magic of Cryx was in her veins, making her an abomination of sorts. He thought of her in the Orgoth vault, recalling how attuned she seemed to be with the dark energy in its depths. What kept her in check? Why had she not devolved into some Cryxian fiend? He thought back to the moment she had reached through the barrier to contact the mysterious sphere. As he did, the hair on the back of his neck pricked up. Likely, if he had done the same thing, it would have killed him.

name: Name
body:
Despite Rosko’s intervention saving the lives of hm and so many of his troops, could she be trusted? Borisyuk cast this thought aside. It did not matter in the end. He was a soldier of Khador. His was to follow orders and nothing else. Today, Cynthia Rosko was an ally.
Of the ancient Orgoth sphere, Borisyuk also wondered. What was it? What power could it offer them? Would it prove to be a new weapon that could turn the tide? Perhaps it was a clue to something greater? Though he dared not allow himself the hope, could it spell the end of the war? There could be little doubt that the chamber meant to hold the sphere all these centuries had taken considerable effort just to contain it. With his own eyes, he had never seen anything like it. In truth, he had to admit to himself, he was more shaken by what he had seen in the depths of the vault than the losses suffered atop it.
"You are wondering, Kapitan." Trailing behind him, his ever-present advisor, the stone-faced Magziev Zariyah Volkova, sensed his mood as was her penchant as a former Greylord. "What is this mystery sphere you saw, yes?"

name: Name
body:
"Not for me to guess." Borisyuk shrugged. "Do you know?"
"I have some idea." Volkova nodded, stifling a yawn. "I have seen similar objects that you have described, though perhaps not so large. If it is what I think, it is powerful but must be combined as a piece of something bigger."
"I doubt we’ll hear much from our friends about that." Borisyuk looked ahead to camp, his stomach growling now. "Cygnar’s intelligence will do with it as they see fit."
"Is shame we could not recover for ourselves?" The lieutenant wondered aloud.
"All that matters now is to prepare for next advance." Borisyuk was more than tired now; he was irritated. The way Volkova spoke—her words were challenging. He fought this feeling, shaking his head. "Unless the Orgoth know it’s gone, they will return. When they do, we must be ready to hold the line again. That is my only concern, Magziev."
"Yes, Kapitan," Volkova demurred. "You will file it in your report, nonetheless?"
"Of course." Squinting, Borisyuk turned toward her at last. "Do you doubt me?"

name: Name
body:
"No, Kapitan." Volkova smiled coolly, her steely eyes fixed to field camp ahead. She ran her fingers along the shaft of her dual-bladed scythe as they marched for the barracks. "I have every confidence you will do all that Khador requires."
***

name: Name
body: Spring, 612 AR Shivering in a cell barely an arm’s width across, one littered with scraps of rancid gore, twelve-year-old Cynthia was utterly alone. Her clothes had been taken on arrival, replaced by torn rags that stank of the last victim to wear them. She had not eaten in days, able only to suckle from a trickle of water in the corner of her cell. The place was often in total darkness yet rarely silent. She had been able to make out that this place belonged to the witch-sisters, as she thought of them. Often, she heard their rasping, bickering banter down the hall in the main room. Today, they had been arguing most of the morning, a ceaseless quarrel over the best way to include Cynthia in a variety of experiments they planned to stage throughout their workshop. Cynthia had never been more terrified in all her life. There was nowhere to run. Her Gift seemed absent, suppressed by rune-covered restraints they had shackled her hands and feet with. The cell was impermeable, even for her. And it was for certain they were going to kill her. When she had been brought here, blindfolded and bound, she had managed only glimpses from under the edges of the cloth. These teased flashes of a range of wicked tools and implements in a workshop that’s only purpose seemed for inflicting cruelty. She’d seen victims splayed against the wall, others reduced to entrail heaps along the floor. As they first led her to her cell, she had seen another unfortunate captive die upon a rack at the center of their chamber.

name: Name
body:
Of the sisters themselves, she had seen almost nothing, leaving their voices and the odd mechanical sounds of their movements to provoke the worst images her imagination could concoct. She often heard the screams of other victims—earlier that day, in fact. But even those had fallen silent soon enough. She could only imagine their fate but tried hard not to.
Somewhere in the chamber down the hall, or perhaps somewhere farther into their workshop, she could hear a machine, like a pipe organ. From time to time, it exhaled a random blast, a protracted tone, faint and sighing. She knew when it was coming because before it did, some poor soul always started screaming. When it stopped, so did the screaming.
Instead of listening, Cynthia drew deeper into herself. There, she found her mother looking back at her, her face wide in terror in the forge in her last moments. Over and over, Cynthia watched her die. The wraith leering at her, chasing them. Then, she saw her father, a man she barely knew, with the same face as the wraith. Sometimes in her dreams he came for her, trying to save her. But it was never enough; she would wake with a start, alone again. She would never see him or her mother again. Cynthia fought back tears as her breathing came in ragged gasps.

name: Name
body:
Faint screams down the hall broke her morbid reverie. Someone being led in chains? She strained to hear. A shuffle and guttural shouts. Moments of silence, then and at last, the pipe organ. It started as a murmur, then began to swell. For two minutes it piped its dark tone, reverberating down the halls, shaking the bones in her chest. When it finally stopped, there was only silence. She was haunted by the experience and felt there something more in that dreadful noise than just its agonizing pitch. It was magic, she was sure, but a kind so alien and depraved that she could not fathom its origin.
"Fear not, for fear is not your killer." Cynthia repeated the words in a whisper, her mother’s adage from days gone by. She had said it many times this morning already. It was not helping, she decided. She would die here. All she had left now was to wait.
***
The royal palace in Caspia soared over the bustling capital, its streets teeming with the industrious pursuits of a million citizens that dwelled, free of outside concern, within its mighty walls. At the center of the palace was the war room, a squat chamber with map-covered walls and deep leather chairs, where for centuries, the fates of untold people had been meticulously debated and decided by those with the power to shape kingdoms.

name: Name
body: It seemed a small ask in such a hallowed place for the formidable authorities gathered to tip the scales in the favor of one very unlucky girl, but here they were. Moreover, the conversation was becoming heated. "Goddammit, that’s not all!" Captain Allister Caine slammed the table with a fist, his cigar nearly falling out of his mouth as he spat the words. "You will remember your place here, Captain." Caine knew the elder Warmaster General Ebonhart was not easily riled but regarded Caine’s outburst with simmering irritation. "We are fighting a war of attrition on three fronts. We simply cannot spare the resources you propose for a single child. Even if she is yours." The torchlit room felt overly warm to Caine, forcing him to loosen his collar. He looked around at the grand tapestries of wars long past, finding no reprieve there. Before him, the council of six sat deadpan except for Bolden Rebald, who was visibly bristling. It certainly came as no surprise to Caine; they had nemeses many times over the years.

name: Name
body:
"The chance your raid succeeds is effectively zero," Rebald hissed, pressing his moustache as he looked at Skell on the map laid out before them on the great table. "Your expedition may as well be gift-wrapped."
"Of all people, Rebald, yeh’d best hope I bring her back." Caine bristled, turning to the man. "It’s as much yer fault as mine she’s there at all."
For his part, Rebald did not dignify the remark, only scoffed.
"I warned you once, Captain." The weathered warmaster rose, clearly on the edge of summoning the guards at the chamber entrance.
"It’s not me yeh need worry about," Caine hissed, barely holding back. "This is about resources, yeh say?"
"What are you getting at?" Ebonheart cut in.
"Even a cynical old bean counter like Rebald here knows the value of a ticking bomb." Caine eyed Rebald with simmering resentment.
"Elaborate." By his expression, Ebonheart had been taken by surprise.
"Cryx found it worth their while to come here for my Cynthia now, didn’t they?" Caine peered around the table to find apprehensive stares greeting him. "Because she’s a right chip off the old block is why. She has the Gift, and she has it in spades. I’ve seen it with my own eyes."

name: Name
body:
Uncomfortable silence followed.
"Did I stutter?" Caine was incensed. "How would yeh relish another Caine playing for the other side?"
Still no answer, but the faces considering his words had become grave.
"We’ve seen it before." Caine paced. "What cost to Cygnar that Cryx was able to take Victoria Haley’s sister? Do yeh know the answer, bean counters?"
Muttered grumbling now, but Caine saw his point was registering.
"How many lives has that Warwitch Deneghra cost us when she might have held the line alongside our major?" Caine moved now behind the backs of his detractors.
"It’s a valid point." Leto leaned in with a measured voice to advise Ebonheart as King Julian’s proxy. His pallor seemed whiter than usual at Caine’s suggestion.
"And a small detachment is all I ask." Caine saw the effect of his words shake the table as he pointed to the map. "I lead them into Skell, quick as a wink and back again. Then she’s back, safe and sound."
Ebonheart narrowed his eyes. "How do you know she’s in Skell? How will you find her?"

name: Name
body:
"We’ve got enough intelligence on Cryx to know that witch’s master, the Lich Lord Asphyxious, is based in Skell. So, call it an educated guess. And once I’m there, I can find her."
"Laughable," Rebald sneered. "You don’t even know where you’re going. If you could actually find her, you’d never get out of Cryx alive. Better operators than you have tried and not returned."
"Yeh lend me that skyship, and they’ll never see us coming." Caine exhaled a cloud of cigar smoke into Rebald’s face. "Or going."
He watched their reaction, shrugs around the table. It appeared nothing could assuage Ebonheart. Caine watched him like a hawk as he shifted in his seat, pulling his beard.
"You ask for our most precious asset as though it were nothing." He shook his head, incredulous.
"Warcasters are yer best assets," Caine countered. "Not only will I bring yer pretty flyer back, but we’ll also make sure Cryx has one less warcaster. Do the math, Warmaster."
"Zero. Zero is the math." Rebald snorted. "She is gone, Allister."

name: Name
body: Caine purpled, giving rise to a sudden flash of runes around him. In an instant, he was across the table. Caine reappeared to grip Rebald’s collar with a single Spellstorm pistol shoved in the spymaster’s face before anyone knew what was happening. "Say it again." Caine hissed, pressing the gun closer to Rebald’s face. "Say it again." When the guards at last pried him off an indignant Rebald, Caine already knew what Ebonheart would say. "Damn your temper, Captain!" The warmaster shook his head in anger. "Rebald is correct, no mater how it burns your ears to hear. You’ll take your leave now, before I have you up on charges. Again." "You’re going to allow that?" A seething Rebald adjusted himself, trying to regain composure. "You don’t make light of a man’s kin, Rebald." Ebonheart answered. "He owed you that one." Caine meanwhile shrugged off his escort’s grasp with a simple teleport. A few leaps later, he reappeared at the grand entrance to the palace in front of two very surprised guards.

name: Name
body:
"Further orders my ass," Caine growled and started walking. As he moved beyond the palace grounds, he joined a steady traffic of pedestrians along one the city’s busy thoroughfares. Alongside him, the lean frame of Ryan, wrapped in a cloak and then Watts, smoking a stogie with a worn canvas jacket, materialized from the crowds. Both wore tricorns pulled low over their eyes.
"Plan B?" Ryan asked with little surprise, her eyes darting through the crowd ahead, never looking to Caine.
"Plan B," Caine agreed, walking with greater purpose now.
"Fekking told ya now, didn’t I?" Watts snorted and shook his head then took a long pull on his stogie.
"Did you actually get it?" Ryan probed.
Caine’s frown broke with a wink. He stopped, letting the bustle move around them as he produced a small object from his breast pocket. It was Rebald’s little black book. He’d seen it many times as the spymaster scribbled his notes in it over and again. If indeed there was a currency that could fund his mission, he was now holding it.

name: Name
body: There wasn’t much time, but he would make it happen. He had to. He needed Ace, his prized warjack for his stealth capabilities. He needed Anastasia di Bray, too—there was no better infiltrator in all Immoren. He needed Kell Bailoch the sniper, the only man he knew who had been to Cryx and lived to tell the tale. And ultimately, he needed the damned skyship. It was time to start calling in favors. It was time to get to work. He replaced the book in his breast pocket and resumed walking. "I’ll be damned." First Watts laughed, then Ryan. "So, where’s Loverboy?" Caine asked, his gleam aimed at Ryan. "Oh, here we go." Ryan rolled her eyes. "I kiss the guy one time." "Well?" "He’s ready to set sail. We’re fully supplied." Ryan paused, smiling. "Clearing the deck to fit our cargo took some doing, but our captain was…motivated." "Then we stick to the plan. Have him bring the ship to the west dock and make ready to take on heavy cargo. We don’t have much time before Rebald gets wise to our little hustle."

name: Name
body:
"Aye-aye," Ryan agreed.
"What about Falk?" Watts paused, rubbing the bare chin of his mutton-chopped face.
"He’ll meet us at the rally point." Caine checked his timepiece then looked up to see Watt’s doubtful frown. "He will. He won’t let me down."
"I guess we’ll see." Watts picked up his pace to match Caine’s.
"We need that skyship," Ryan added. "It really is our only way in."
"I know." Caine smiled, though he did not feel any happiness. A simmering rage burned in him now, loosed by Rebald’s words. He would not let Cynthia down, no matter the cost.
***

name: Name
body:
Deep beneath the fortress walls of the main Cygnaran Armory compound in Caspia, Caine and the gun mage Bastian Falk walked a long stone corridor, both of them at ease and very much not at ease. Here, the armory’s sublevels became a vast labyrinth radiating in all directions from a series of central lifts they had left well behind them. In all, it was a tomb-like antiseptic affair, the cylindrical tunnels they walked forming a precision stonework fully twenty feet high with suspended gas lamps along the ceiling and inset rail lines running central along the floor.
Caine had already lost count of the alcoves along each corridor they traveled, some presenting as short junctions to further corridors while others ended abruptly in heavy vault doors.  Workshops, forges, and storage lockups of every sort lay behind those doors, some silent and secured by padlock while others had been thrown wide open, resonating with the sound of men and machines at work inside.
They were now several floors deep into the facility—they did not belong there, and they were trying their best to seem like they did. The gun mage Falk had his tricorn tilted back and displayed a casual smile on his slender, bespectacled face. The pair strolled along under the pretense of a jovial conversation, though it chafed Caine something fierce with every step they took.

name: Name
body:
"He’s in there." Falk smiled, pausing at last before an otherwise nondescript alcove to the right of the corridor. Twenty feet deep, the alcove ended in thick vault double doors braced with a crossbar and an imposing padlock. The alcove met the rail line with tracks of its own; these continuing beneath the doors. There was no sound beyond. Indeed, the alcove’s light flickered, leaving the doors in a pall of alternating light and shadow.
As Caine looked on, the sound of footsteps echoed down the high-ceilinged hall from the direction they had just come. Shouts rose then—something large was being moved on steel wheels that creaked with effort. A steamjack was coming, too, with telltale heavy footfalls and hissing steam pistons. The arc of the corridor soon revealed the source as they turned around to meet it.
A flatbed cart approached, laden with a partial warjack wreck, attended by a work crew of six engineers in worn jump suits and an Engines East new model steamjack polished nearly to a shine. The cargo appeared to be an old Centurion, inert, rusted, and in a horrible state of disrepair.

name: Name
body: Perhaps fallen in battle, the thing had been beaten to scrap or nearly so, now on its way to some workshop for repair or, far more likely, salvage. Caine nodded at the men as they passed, noting the deep impression of hammer blows across the wreck’s broad shoulders, chest, and visored head. The latter had burst with the attack, the internal components of its face brutally exposed. For their part, the engineers noted Caine and Falk talking, faint recognition registering in their passing. "What a mess." Falk broadened his smile and chuckled to the men, then grimaced at Caine as the they continued down the corridor’s arc and out of sight. "Come on." "I can’t sense him." Caine felt beyond the alcove’s door with his thoughts. "Are you sure that’s where they’ve moved him?" "That’s the word." "Why bring him here?" At the end of shadowy alcove was a sign above the doors: WORKSHOP 18. "The cloak. Strangeways wants a look. This time, he’s going to figure it out." "Fek me," Caine hissed. In fifteen years, Ace’s cloaking device had never been duplicated. The engineer responsible for the unique gadget that conveyed near-invisibility for itself and those nearby, Clancy Chaucer, was long dead, the blueprints for his enigmatic device destroyed in the same laboratory fire that ended his life. This had left the precise formulation of the alchemical components within the cloak’s manifold unknown, although the topic of frequent speculation.

name: Name
body:
Every few years since, some bright engineer within the foundry got it in their head to pry Ace open and attempt to reverse engineer the cloak. All such efforts had gone nowhere, as the risk of damaging the liquid canisters within the device loomed. Yet Arlen Strangeways was resourceful indeed, and Caine conceded he might well have a shot at solving it if he’d taken up the challenge. This was just bad timing. The truth was that Ace’s cloak had made the difference between life and death for Caine countless times and there would be no infiltration of Skell without it. Full stop.
"If Ace is in pieces, we’re dead in the water here." Caine probed again for his bonded warjack’s cortex. There was only the silence of the tomb behind those doors. Caine licked his lips. Ace may simply be dormant—or his cortex could be gone entirely. Caine simply couldn’t tell from here.
"Sorry," Falk said as they approached the doors.
"Eh, I appreciate yeh stickin’ yer neck out for me just the same, Bastian." Caine produced a lock pick from his sleeve. "Let’s see about these doors first,"

name: Name
body:
"It’s the very least I can do. After what you did for my husband?" Falk watched Caine grasp the lock and insert his pick. "Uh, can’t you just, you know…"
"Teleport?" Caine smiled bitterly. "I use magic here, the rune plate wards embedded in the walls of this place will trip the alarm. Yeh want to have to shoot yer way back out?"
"Not so much." Falk scowled, visibly disturbed. "As you were."
Sounds of movement, then, echoed down hall. Caine heard the grind of another cart coming along the track, raised voices in tow.
"Check it out." Caine remained focused on his work as Falk peered round the corner. "Is that our engineer friends?"
"Guards." Falk watched a moment longer. "In an awful hurry. They’ve a cart, and there’s an agent with them. He’s CRS, no doubt about it."
Caine frowned at the news and removed his pick; he’d been unsuccessful after several attempts. He moved for the corner, daring a glance from beside Falk. Indeed, a large contingent was making its way to them with purpose, speaking loudly enough to be heard from this distance. A stern-faced man in gray led the way, nearly at a jog.

name: Name
body:
"Hurry." The agent produced keys from his belt without breaking stride. "Rebald wants that cortex, and he wants it yesterday."
"I suppose I had this coming." Caine rubbed his eyes. "Rebald knows full well I need Ace after I pretty much laid out the whole plan to the War Council."
"We’re in a corner here. What we do?" Falk pressed his back to the wall. "Surrender?"
"Never." Caine ducked back to look at the failure of the lock as the agent’s keys jangled louder on approach. "If nothing else, at least we’re sure Ace is here now."
"You got a plan? Tell me you got a plan."
"I’m working on it." Caine took a deep breath. "How far back you reckon the gatehouse was? With all the guards?"
"Is this part of the plan? Three levels up. A twenty-minute walk?"
"Or a ten-minute run." Caine listened to the echo of footsteps now practically on top of them now. "Brace yerself now. First time pack’s a punch."
Falk stiffened. "I don’t know about this plan anymore."
Caine pictured the corridor in his mind, specifically a point where they had just been. Dead center over the tracks, maybe a foot off the ground. He listened to the guards’ approach, heard them reach the corner.

name: Name
body: Then…

name: Name
body:
Caine and Falk vanished. Caine pulled them through the void to the other side, now ten yards behind the guards and the agent, just in time to watch them round the corner for the alcove where the two of them had just been standing. Beside him, Falk swayed on his feet, his eyes bulging.
"You weren’t joking," Falk groaned, watching the guards turn the corner, their cart the last in line. "I wish you’d told me that was part of the plan. What now?"
Overhead, a klaxon bell began to ring, blaring down the corridor. Caine’s magic had indeed tripped the alarm, but he was ready for it.
"Cover the hall. First sign of anyone, give a shout, yeh?"
Falk nodded and hunkered down behind a steel oil drum.
Caine rounded the corner back into the alcove, both Spellstorm pistols drawn and aimed at the backs of the guards as they waited for the CRS agent to open the door.
"Gents. Drop yer weapons and raise yer hands." Caine grinned, cocking his pistols for effect. As the agent raised a hand toward his breast pocket, Caine shook his head. "Come on now. Yeh know who I am."

name: Name
body:
The agent frowned then slowly raised his hands. He cocked his head to the ringing of the alarm. "You really think you’re getting out of here now?"
"That is kind of Ace’s thing." Caine pointed to the opened door and the workshop beyond it with a pistol. "Everyone inside, let’s go."
One by one, the guards filed into the dimly lit workshop, hands raised high.
Caine scanned the chamber with one wary eye on his captive audience. The narrow room had been left with work in progress; tools, spot lamps, chemistry vials, and a table set up with dozens of sample jars. Central to it all, Ace stood, secured within a warjack harness and a hoist, galvanic wires extending from his cloak’s manifold to a vaned generator.
Beyond the inert warjack was a chimneyed forge along the far wall with a half-cord of wood and a hopper of coal neatly stacked by a bellows. Now in plain sight of Ace, Caine wondered why he could not sense his bonded warjack’s mind until he saw the shining metal sphere on a workbench. Ace’s cortex. Absent its body, the mechanika marvel of Ace’s mind would sleep or something close to it.

name: Name
body:
"You men—" Caine led with his pistols, beckoning two of his captives to approach. His eyes darted to the cortex, then he nodded at the open hatch on Ace’s back. "—put that back where it belongs."
"Is this a joke?" The agent smirked as the guards struggled with the cortex. "You’ll never get it running before—"
Caine pressed the barrel of one pistol against the agent’s lips and watched his eyes cross until they looked like they might pop out of his skull.
"Well, not with that attitude, eh?" Caine looked to the remaining guards. "You, stuff a rag in this one’s mouth so we don’t have to suffer his claptrap any longer. The rest of you, help me get the old boy moving, will yeh?"
Without a word of resistance, the remaining guards came around to Ace’s backside to ignite and stoke his furnace. In short order, smoke wisps began to curl from his stacks, steam starting to build. As the cortex settled into place, Caine waived the men back and shut the hatch. Ace’s eyes began to flicker behind the visor of his face.

name: Name
body: Though the warjack could not yet turn to regard him, Caine felt Ace’s mind at the edge of his own. Ace responded, his thoughts an impression of familiarity and surprise over actual words. I missed yeh, too. Care for a little fun? Ace emoted by flexing shoulders until a shrug slowly formed as his neck pistons pressurized. His head turned in slow motion, looking round the room, then back to Caine. "We need to sneak yeh out of here." Caine spoke aloud now in a conspiratorial tone as he leaned close to Ace’s visor. "So yeh can help me get my girl back." Ace clanged twice in affirmation, beginning to flex his arms. As steam continued to build, the warjack’s stacks huffed with smoke. Then, Falk was at the doorway, his scarf pulled up to his eyes to avoid being recognized by the guards. "Incoming. South hall. Full squad. Guns out." Falk was out of breath, but he quickly noted the CRS agent’s rag-stuffed mouth. "Everything all right in here?" "Dandy." Caine said. "Can yeh buy us some time? Ace is a little stiff yet."

name: Name
body:
"I’ll figure out something." Falk drew his weapon from its side holster. Then he grabbed a vial from the nearest table and examined it, swirling a colorful green liquid around. "This looks important enough. Mine now, then. Meet you at the rally point?"
"The rally point, aye." Caine nodded, watching as Ace stretched his legs, straining at his harness. "Try not to get caught? I still need yeh."
"Gonna do my best. Part of the plan, right?" Falk dipped out of the doorway. A few seconds later, a shot rang out in the corridor. Shots fired in return. Then Caine could hear the sound of Falk running away, taunting his pursuers, with shouts fading down the length of the northern corridor. The sound of men running in armor clamored past the door and faded away as well.
"Gentlemen." Caine ushered his captives to move behind Ace, sensing his prized warjack was ready to move. "We’ll see ourselves out. Someone will be along shortly to retrieve yeh."
He pulled the release on Ace’s harness, and the warjack’s leg pistons hissed as they bore the full weight of the warjack. As Ace stomped toward the door, the shadowy umbrella of his cloak shimmered to life, covering the warjack in a haze, making him little more than a shadow.

name: Name
body:
Caine followed but not before closing the door to the workshop and locking its great padlock. Satisfied that the guards were trapped, he tossed the key down the length of the corridor and ran. Ahead of him, a shadowy Ace was already into a sprint.
***

name: Name
body:
Haphazard, ramshackle, and derelict, the hovels and slums that made up Skell were crowded and piled upon each other, as if competing to be closer to the great palace of the Dragonfather that dominated the city’s center. Clustered around a domed edifice large enough to contain the most titanic creature on Caen was an expanse of connected turrets, temples, and towers within which the dark machinations of Cryx were birthed and reared. It was in one such tower, a jagged spire jabbing skyward from the edge of the necrofactorium enclave, that the macabre tones of the horrible machine haunted Cynthia.
"Tell me of your progress," a woman’s voice demanded, as stern as it was silky, echoing down the hall to Cynthia’s cell. Cynthia perked up, listening closely from the bottom of her cell door. She knew that voice and the chill it gave her all too well. It was her abductor, the undead warwitch Deneghra.
"She is lively," said the witch-sister Sekka; this was followed by a mechanical wheezing. It was a peculiar sound Cynthia heard at odd intervals since she had been brought here, making the creature’s actual mood difficult to gauge. "Very lively."

name: Name
body:
A rasp then from the witch sister, Lynak. It was an equally strange sound: guttural and interrupted by frequent wet coughing. "F-fearless, she thinks."
Cynthia had seen precious little of these creatures over the last few days, left alone in darkness as she was most of the time. The occasional and partial glimpses she had gathered through the grates of her cell only added to their horror. Both limped with disturbing irregularities; both seemed a patchwork of iron and flesh brought together in an unknown design. The only thing she was certain of was that they were female and referred to each other as sister.
"She resists the necrothereum. It seems not to her taste yet," said Sekka, her voice now a trailing hiss of disappointment.
"Nothing is to her taste, of course," Lynak lamented with a mocking tone between hacking coughs. "She’s not taken a morsel since she arrived. Not a single bite."
"Good," Deneghra answered. "Then she’s ready for the rack."
***
With its reinforced walls and newly constructed gun emplacements, Point Bourne sometimes felt more like a fortress than the thriving trade center it had been before the Thornwood War. But somehow the merchants and traders who made their livings among the terraced locks of the river town managed business as usual, even amidst the frequent rumble of artillery fire rising from the thick forest to the north.

name: Name
body:
Anastasia di Bray darted between the shadows of dusk, moving from alley to street and back again nearly at a sprint, always without ever being seen. It was an impressive pace she kept, wrapped tightly in her cloak, as Caine watched with a lit stogie from the most familiar of all his haunts: tenement rooftops. He saw she was nearly to her destination, though he could not let her reach it.
With a glance at the tenements across the road, Caine eased his Gift to pull him there, slipping through the darkness of the space in-between places, reappearing at the edge of the next rooftop. Just below him, Anastasia paused at the corner to peer around it with caution. Caine looked to her destination: a town home three stories tall and finely adorned by Cygnaran standards. The neighborhood was upper class, each building better appointed than the last. Accordingly, patrols of soldiery moved through at intervals to keep the riff-raff out. Caine meanwhile watched the civilian traffic move to and fro, counting no less than five agents  just waiting to snatch her up. With a breath, he eased his Gift to bring him to street level.

name: Name
body:
"I wouldn’t go in there if I were you." Caine appeared next to Anastasia, crushing the butt of his stogie with a heel. "It’s a trap."
Anastasia wheeled on Caine’s remark with a blade already drawn and aimed at his throat. He was ready for the move after a lifetime of teleporting behind people. He grabbed the offending wrist while reaching for the other as it erupted from her cloak, similarly equipped.
"Caine?" Anastasia’s snarl became shock.
"I’ve been looking for you, darlin’." Caine cocked his head, smiling. "Missed you by a step at your meet up, but that’s what tipped me off to yer little dilemma here. Yeh picked up a tail, and they was having a little chat about yeh with some very interested parties. Let’s just say I asked them nicely where yeh was going."
A patrol of Cygnaran long gunners walked past the corner. Still holding her by the wrists, Caine instinctively pulled Anastasia into a lover’s embrace. Sensing the play, Anastasia leaned into it, planting a passionate kiss on his lips. The passing soldiers paid them enough attention for a catcall and little else. When they were gone, the pair let go.

name: Name
body:
"Good kiss." Anastasia shook her head. "Cheap stogies."
"Never mind that." Caine smiled. "You’re expecting to find Daniels in there, right?"
"Yes,"
"He ain’t." Caine looked to the town home. "But he did leave a surprise for yeh."
"Where is he then?" Anastasia eyed the home suspiciously, her gaze lingering on the lights in the window.
"Boarding a steamer, I reckon. With what he owes ya. Seen him myself."
"Where? Which dock?"
"If I take yeh to him, would you consider a favor?" Caine patted his pockets, looking for another stogie. "I wouldn’t ask if it wasn’t important."
"What sort of favor?" Anastasia slipped into her native Llaelese, a seductive flow she knew full well Caine could speak when pressed.
"I need a plan to break into Skell. My daughter has been taken, and I mean to get her back."
"You’re kidding, yes?" Anastasia barked a laugh as she put her hands on hips.
For his part, Caine could only shrug and light his new cigar with a match.
"You’re not kidding." Anastasia blinked, slipping back to Llaelese.

name: Name
body:
Caine held her stare, chomping his stogie.
"No one is insane enough to do what you’re talking about." The idea played across her face, and Caine saw a little gleam in her eyes then. "You can’t afford me."
"Had a feeling yeh might say that." Caine produced Rebald’s little black book. He proceeded to open it and show her a single page entry.
"I stand corrected." Anastasia eyes widened. "Is this really what I think it is?"
"It is. Help me, and it’s yours."
"What is her name?"
"Cynthia."
"I can’t wait to meet her." Anastasia smiled.
***

name: Name
body:
Even for the cutthroat hive of pirates, miscreants, and ne’re-do-wells that comprised Five Fingers, the Chum Bucket was a flophouse against which all others could claim at least a modicum of respectability, and it more than lived up to its name.
"This is your last chance." The shout came from behind the door upstairs, the third in a row of five along a balcony overlooking the decrepit dining hall. It was a man’s voice, steady and serious. "I come out this door, I’m going to kill every last man with a gun pointed at me."
Caine looked around the tavern, knowing full well it was no idle threat. The voice belonged to a famously despicable, though unmatched, assassin and sniper: Kell Bailoch. Despite this, bold laughter rang throughout the room, contrasted by no small amount of whimpering.
For his part, Caine sat quietly watching the drama unfold from the filth-covered bar while he nursed a pint of stout. The bartender had fled. Caine noted that half the patrons were ducking for cover under tables, chairs, and each other while the other half had just been revealed as hired gunmen of a rough looking sort. All had weapons drawn and trained on the door.

name: Name
body:
In all, Caine counted twenty-three gunmen, all amused by Kell’s ultimatum. He watched the men laughing among themselves, even raised his pint to them with a knowing smile. If they were laughing, they obviously didn’t know who they were dealing with. By the looks of them, he would guess they were men loyal to one of the high captains who ran the city from the shadows. As he’d recently learned, one in particular had beef with Kell. It appeared they meant to settle it just as he’d arrived. The timing was unfortunate.
"Gentlemen." With a final pull of his stout, Caine stood from the bar and turned to the gunmen. "Any of you mind if I have a word with your friend upstairs before the shooting starts? I’ve come a long way to see him."
More laughter as the gunmen looked him over. Caine saw no recognition there either, only smug amusement. The standards of the crime syndicate that dominated Five Fingers had clearly slipped of late if these mooks were the best they could muster.
"Get in line," the leader of the gang barked with an ugly smirk behind a ragged beard. "We got here first."

name: Name
body:
"Be that as it may." Caine pulled back his duster to reveal his holstered Spellstorm pistols. "I wasn’t really asking, pal. I was just giving yeh a chance."
Eyes went wide all around the tavern as every gun was suddenly turned for Caine. But it was far too late to try to get the drop on someone like Caine, especially with his Spellstorms already in hand. As he felt those familiar grips press into his palms, he reached into the deepest part in his mind, the very source of his Gift, as he had done so many times before, pulling forth incandescent runes that began to encircle him and his weapons as well.
As they did, time beyond Caine slowed. The men around him held their expressions in a disquieting pause, their movements slowing almost to a stop. The room became deadly quiet to Caine, his own movements a blur to those looking at him. Then, as his fingers found the triggers in that perfect moment, Caine opened fire.
In a simple sweep, he aimed high to low, left to right across the room. His weapons erupted with glitter-laced fire that found their marks in less than a second of real time. His wrists flicked a subtle dip, freeing his breaches to expend their loaders, his hands pulling his pistols down to his hips, engaging each with a new six-round loader before another flick snapped them closed and brought them back up to aim.

name: Name
body:
He picked up where he left off, tracing high to low, left to right across the tavern to catch the remaining targets. Each shot sent sparks flying as the rune-etched bullets from his twin Spellstorms shattered gun barrels and splintered rifle stocks, disarming each and every gunman of whatever weapon they had brought to bear. Then Caine exhaled, let his Gift fade, and dropped his Spellstorms back into their holsters as he sat down at the bar. Real time returned; Caine reached once more for his stout, the peppery scent of gunpowder filling the air. Sound returned then too, as the shouts of twenty-three gunmen and every remaining patron in the tavern scrambled over one another to vacate the premises as if it were nothing less than a building on fire.
Upstairs, Kell opened the door, his rifle tracing left to right to find no one but Caine left in the bar.
"Allister Caine," Kell shouted down, his rifle trained. "I might have rather been left with a room full of Syndicate goons."
"Awe, c’mon now, Kell. Yer not still sore over Ternon Crag, are yeh?" Caine turned in his seat to raise his tankard, smiling. "Call it even. Yeh don’t even have to thank me."

name: Name
body:
"I could have handled them." Kell sniffed, then his scarred face relented as he emerged.
"Pull up a stool." Caine took a drink. "We’ve got business to discuss, and there ain’t much time."
Kell lowered his rifle and descended to join Caine at the bar. He sampled an abandoned mead and looked around. "Hope it’s better than Ternon Crag."
"Well, I can promise you, there won’t be farrow." Caine’s expression hardened. "I need a sniper."
"Obviously," Kell sipped, unimpressed. "Why me?"
"I need a sniper who’s been to Cryx and lived to tell the tale."
"Forget it." Kell sipped again, his cool grey eyes meeting Caine’s over the rim of his tankard. "I ain’t going back there. Not for all the money in the world."
"Then you’re in luck, because I don’t have two crowns to my name." Caine held his gaze.
Kell scoffed, finished his mead. "You wasted your time coming here."
He pushed back his stool, readying to leave.
"Slow down, now. I’ve been doing some reading. From this little black book that knows all kinds of things." Caine tapped his left earlobe. "I know why that gang wants yeh dead. I know yeh shot the ear of the head of the high captain they work for."

name: Name
body:
"Watch your mouth, Caine."
"I also know about the bounty he put on yer head." Caine looked over the bar, taking a slow sip. "And the beating he laid on yer mum, am I right?"
Kell’s expression narrowed. "A book really told you this?"
"Some. I know she won’t let yeh kill the man on account of she works for him, and it’s all she’s got. She made you promise, didn’t she? Family ties, they bind—am I right?"
Kell seethed and said nothing.
"I get it," Caine said. "I got ties of my own. The whole reason I’m headed to Cryx is to pull my little girl out of Skell."
Kell blanched, then laughed without humor, an altogether ugly sound. "You ain’t right in the head, are you?"
